title: Rules everywhere
hook: the Sikh rahit, the Buddhist precepts, Franklin's virtues: ways of life written down so you can see where you stand
tomorrow: God takes his people to court, with mountains for a jury. the verdict?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: a little rule. Benedict, once poisoned for being too strict, wrote a rule with nothing harsh in it. Today, a week of lines comes back, and a few more rules.

The black dots were his faults. Benjamin Franklin tells it in his autobiography. He wanted to live without a single fault, so he listed twelve virtues, temperance, silence, order and the rest. Then a Quaker friend told him people found him proud, so Franklin added a thirteenth: humility. He gave each virtue a page in a little book, with a column for every day of the week, and each slip got a black spot. The surprise was how many spots there were.
screen: `TWELVE VIRTUES.` → `ONE MORE: HUMILITY.` → `A BLACK SPOT FOR EACH SLIP.` → `SO MANY SPOTS.`

segments.voice: He never finished the book clean. But he wrote that he was a better and happier man for trying. Franklin's little book is a homemade version of something traditions also do: write the way of life down, so you can see where you stand. Sikhs have the Rahit Maryada, a written code of Sikh conduct that includes daily prayers and how the community lives together. Buddhists keep the five precepts: not killing, not stealing, no sexual misconduct, no false speech, no intoxicants. They're called training rules, taken on by the person who says them, not commands handed down. Here's the teaching under all three. Written down, a rule stops being a vague good intention. It becomes something you can look at, keep, slip on, and come back to. That's this week in one picture. Greening, her music, my anthology, read it aloud, my own, a little rule. Each was a line you could carry. A rule is just those lines, written where you'll see them.
screen: `FRANKLIN'S LITTLE BOOK.` · `THE SIKH RAHIT MARYADA.` · `FIVE PRECEPTS: TRAINING RULES.` · `A RULE YOU CAN SEE AND KEEP.` · then, large: `WRITTEN DOWN.`

segments.voice: Count this week's lines on your fingers, one per finger: greening, her music, my anthology, read it aloud, my own, a little rule. Stop on the one you'd most want written somewhere you'll see it every day, and stay with it until the time is up.
Rules everywhere: the Sikh rahit, the Buddhist precepts, Franklin's little book, each a way of life written down.
Here's the line: written down, so a good intention becomes something you can see. A week of lines, kept.

howItsDone: The Sikh Rahit Maryada sets out a written code of Sikh conduct; lay Buddhists take on the five precepts by reciting them as training rules; others keep personal rules, as Franklin did with his chart of virtues.

fork.setup: your friend's new year list lives only in her head and has faded by February. she asks why some people bother writing a rule. what fits today?

chat.says: told theo i'm writing a rule of life. he went quiet. rules ran his whole childhood. what do i say?
options: mine's like the precepts: training rules I take on, a mirror I chose.
tell him rules are good for everyone, and he'll come around in time.
agree that all written rules are control, and quietly drop yours.
chat.meaning: Buddhist precepts are training rules the person takes on; Franklin's book was a mirror he made for himself. A chosen rule isn't someone's control.

tie.story: Franklin marked his own slips in a little book, and Buddhists take on the precepts themselves as training rules.
tie.friend: Zoe can tell Theo her rule is chosen and hers, not the kind that ran his childhood, and leave him room.
tie.you: what intention of yours would change if you wrote it down?
